history.heading: Heart of the Maya world
paragraphs: Guatemala was a centre of the Maya civilisation for thousands of years. Great cities such as Tikal, El Mirador and Kaminaljuyú flourished; Tikal, in the northern Petén rainforest, was one of the most powerful Maya cities, at its height between around 200 and 900 CE. After the decline of the lowland cities, highland Maya kingdoms such as the K'iche' and Kaqchikel remained strong.

history.heading: Spanish colony
paragraphs: Pedro de Alvarado conquered the highland kingdoms from 1524. Guatemala became the centre of the Captaincy General of Guatemala, covering most of Central America. Its colonial capital, Antigua Guatemala, was abandoned after earthquakes in 1773 and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.heading: Independence and dictatorships
paragraphs: Guatemala became independent in 1821 and fully separate from the Central American federation in 1839. Liberal and conservative strongmen ruled for much of the 19th and early 20th centuries, while coffee and banana plantations, notably those of the US United Fruit Company, dominated the economy.
A democratic period from 1944 brought reforms, including land redistribution under President Jacobo Árbenz. In 1954 a CIA-backed coup overthrew him.

history.heading: Civil war and peace
paragraphs: A civil war from 1960 to 1996 between the military government and leftist guerrillas killed around 200,000 people, most of them indigenous Maya civilians. A UN-backed truth commission found that the state committed acts of genocide against Maya communities in the early 1980s. Rigoberta Menchú, a K'iche' activist, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1992.

Peace accords were signed in 1996. In 2015 corruption investigations by a UN-backed commission (CICIG) led to the resignation and arrest of the president. Anti-corruption candidate Bernardo Arévalo won the 2023 election and took office in 2024 after attempts to block his inauguration.

culture.heading: Maya heritage
paragraphs: About 40 percent or more of Guatemalans are indigenous, mostly Maya, the highest share in Central America; more than 20 Mayan languages are spoken, along with Spanish, the official language. Religion blends Catholicism and evangelical Protestantism with Maya traditions.
Traditional handwoven textiles (traje) with distinctive patterns identify villages. The Popol Vuh, the sacred book of the K'iche' Maya, is a masterpiece of indigenous literature.

culture.heading: Traditions and food
paragraphs: Holy Week in Antigua, with elaborate carpets of coloured sawdust and flowers, is world famous. Giant kite festivals mark the Day of the Dead. Guatemalan food is based on maize, beans and chilli, with dishes such as pepián (a spiced stew) and tamales. Writer Miguel Ángel Asturias won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1967.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Guatemala is a presidential republic with a president elected for a single four-year term and a unicameral Congress. Corruption, organised crime and the influence of elites on institutions, including the courts and prosecutor's office, are central political issues. Guatemala maintains a territorial claim to part of Belize, submitted to the International Court of Justice.

economy.heading: Largest economy in Central America
paragraphs: Guatemala has the largest economy in Central America. It exports coffee, sugar, bananas, cardamom (it is the world's largest exporter), textiles and palm oil. Remittances from Guatemalans in the United States are very large, making up around a fifth of GDP.
Despite macroeconomic stability, poverty and malnutrition are widespread, especially in indigenous rural areas, and inequality is high. The currency is the quetzal, named after the national bird.
